newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall, dollar gains as bond yield nears 7 percent.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall, dollar gains as bond yield nears 7 percent.

text.p: Stocks fell but the dollar rose Wednesday as long-term interest rates rose near the key 7 percent level.

The Dow Jones industrial average lost 18.88 points to 6,877.68 after falling 70 points earlier in the session. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,532 to 931 on active volume of 535 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond lost 10/32, or $3.13 on a $1,000 bond, and its yield stood at 6.99 percent, compared with 6.96 percent on Tuesday.
"We're nearly at 7 percent on the long bond and we're certainly not going to make much progress while that's the case," said Harry Laubscher, an analyst at Tucker Anthony.
"For now, people seem very concerned about next week's (Federal Reserve) meeting," Laubscher said.
Bond yields of 7 percent tend to draw funds into bonds and away from stocks.

Contributing to the worries about interest rates was the government's report of a 0.3 percent rise in the Consumer Price Index for February, up from 0.1 percent in January. Economists had forecast a 0.2 percent increase.

Economists said the data probably would not change views at the Fed, the nation's central bank, whose policy-makers meet on March 25 to decide whether to raise short-term rates in a bid to ward off inflation.

"The February CPI report won't change any minds about what the Fed will do," Bruce Steinberg, manager of Macroeconomics at Merrill Lynch said in a research note. "We expect the Fed to leave policy unchanged, but we admit it is almost a 50-50 call at this point," he said.
While stock traders remain divided on the outlook for interest rates, their attitude appears far clearer regarding technology stocks, which have been punished since peaking in late January.
That trend continued, with the Nasdaq composite index falling to its lowest since early November 1996. The Nasdaq lost 20.05 points, or 1.58 percent, to 1,249.29.
A broad array of high-tech stocks fell, including semiconductor and computer makers as well as computer network companies.
In currency trading, the dollar rose to 1.6810 German marks and 122.82 Japanese yen from 1.6738 marks and 122.45 yen late Tuesday.
Soybean prices rose on talk of exports to China, while corn and wheat prices closed higher on worries about spring flooding.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, May soybeans closed 8 cents a bushel higher at $8.39 as China was rumoured to have bought 50,000 metric tons of soybeans for April shipment.
May wheat closed up 7-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.91, with traders citing concerns that the expected flooding in the upper Midwest could delay spring wheat plantings.
May corn closed up 2-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.03-1/4, with concerns centred on possible flooding delaying corn planting and forcing a shift of planned corn acreage to soybeans.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index fell 24.6 points to 4,332.2. In Tokyo, the Nikkei average rose 48.51 points to 18,493.71.
